text: ne to acute rejection with ciclosporin than with tacrolimus.16 It has been suggested that tacrolimus be substituted for ciclosporin in those patients suffering persistent rejection, or adverse effects associated with ciclosporin,17 or with hyperlipidaemia or hypertension.18 Microemulsifying ciclosporin may be associated with less rejection than the oil-based formulation.19 The use of mycophenolate mofetil instead of azathioprine in triple therapy has been shown to reduce mortality and rejection in the first year after heart transplantation,20 and a retrospective review21 concluded that the advent of myc- ophenolate mofetil has contributed to improved survival in cardiac transplant recipients. Although lower mycophe- nolic acid (MPA) concentrations may be associated with an increased allograft rejection,22 there appears to be no benefit in monitoring MPA concentrations beyond the first year in heart transplant recipients,23 and MPA levels may be affected by concomitant immunosuppression, see Im- munosuppressants under Interactions of Mycophenolate, p.1837. Many variations of regimens exist, and different drugs have been substituted or used adjunctively in order to de- crease the doses, and thus alleviate the adverse effects as- sociated with calcineurin inhibitors and/or corticosteroids. Substituting cyclophosphamide for azathioprine for 6 weeks after transplantation is reported to reduce the devel- opment of anti-muromonab-CD3 antibodies from induc- tion therapy.24 Substitution of mycophenolate mofetil with intravenous pulse cyclophosphamide for 4 months post- transplantation appeared to decrease the risk of rejection in a small, non-randomised study in sensitised allograft re- cipients.25 Alternative adjunctive therapies are the proliferation sig- nal inhibitors, sirolimus and everolimus,2,9 which allow for use of lower doses of calcineurin inhibitors, thus pre- serving renal function; however, long-term data are limit- ed, and there is little experience with these drugs in paedi- atric patients. Use of sirolimus with ciclosporin and corticosteroids markedly reduced the incidence of acute rejection in a small open-label study.26 However, the use of sirolimus with mycophenolate mofetil was associated with a higher than expected incidence of acute rejection in car- diac transplant patients switched from calcineurin inhibi- tors to this combination.27 It has been suggested that the high doses of corticosteroids used increase the risk of cardiac adverse events in the long- er term, and protocols that wean patients from corticoster- oids after 6 months postoperatively have been used,28,29 without apparent increases in infection or rejection.
